sections.content: The content is easy, and you won't have to worry about memorising anything, it's fairly general and pretty interesting. The slides are easy to understand, and the professor shows quite a few YouTube videos during class, which makes grasping the concepts way faster.
sections.teaching: The professor is very approachable and explains everything really well. Even if you miss a class or two, you won't have trouble understanding the new content, since most sessions aren't really related to the previous ones.
sections.grading: The exams are MCQs, and most of the questions are pretty straightforward. The final did have 2 short answer questions, which needed to be answered directly from the slide content.
sections.workload: There's a midterm, final exam, and a group presentation. All of this is doable. Also, there's no attendance, just class participation. You can enter class a little late, ask a question or answer one, and just tick the participation sheet.

sections.content: Compared to my friend's class, I think Professor Chen didn't teach much content.
sections.teaching: She's a very nice person, very patient, and answer any question.
sections.grading:
The grading criteria are participation, midterm, and final exams. Of course, there's also lab work.

We have to ask a lot of questions in class to get participation, which has caused the course progress to be disrupted. Also, at the beginning of the semester, she said three participation cards would get full marks, but I don't know when that number increased, and  I don't know how many participation cards are actually needed for full marks.

The exams are mostly memory-based, which results in everyone getting high scores.

For the group project, 5 people needed to create  40-page PowerPoint presentation. I put in a lot of effort, but the final grade difference was very small.

I was expecting A- but ended up with B+, which is acceptable, and that's why I gave this course and Prof Chen B...?
sections.workload: Acceptable

sections.content: Honestly, it’s pretty low-key — either show up to the lectures or catch up with the recordings later. The first few sessions might feel a bit all over the place because it’s not always clear what’ll show up on the exam. But in the end, it really just comes down to going through the slides. There’s zero math involved — it's mostly just about grasping the concepts.
sections.teaching: On the bright side, the professor herself is wonderful — super approachable, genuinely helpful, and quick to reply to emails. You can tell she really cares about teaching and puts a lot of heart into it. She's always open to chatting or answering questions after class, too. Honestly, despite the grading quirks, I genuinely enjoyed the course and had a great time with the material.
sections.grading:
That said, the grading structure is pretty frustrating. The project breakdown feels oddly designed — there's a 2-point component based on peer evaluations, but it wasn't even required for everyone, so only a portion of the class actually submitted ratings. My group ended up scoring poorly on that section, and I honestly don't get why classmates should have any say in our grade. The exams, though, are totally reasonable — nothing strays from the slides or what she covers in lectures.

There's no attendance policy, but you do need to answer or ask around 8 questions throughout the semester to max out your participation marks. She threw in quite a few easy points toward the end, so honestly, you could skip most classes and still walk away with full credit there. It's absolute grading — I think 85% and above is an A+, with the B range sitting roughly between 70–80%. Maybe that explains why she's so tough on the project side.
sections.workload: Workload-wise, it's super light. There's just one group project—about a 10-page paper plus a presentation—and absolutely no homework assigned throughout the semester. I'm not entirely sure if the lab section counts toward that, but even if it does, it's pretty chill. They do have attendance quizzes, but you're allowed to miss at least one without any penalty.

sections.grading:
There are one exam for the course and one for the lab. The course exam is just rote memorizing. Everything tested is mentioned in the ppt slides, so if you can remember all the contents (The exams are non-cumulative so there are around 8 ppt with about 40 pages for mid term and final) you are good.
The lab exam will cover all the tools they have introduced, but it is 100% mc and not too difficult.
You do get good grade for the project as long as the idea is solid and the proposal follows the guidelines exactly. Just try to integrate the class content in the presentation as much as possible.
sections.workload:
Workload is low until the very end of the course. There is no assignment but a group presentation at the end of semester. Group project has several stages, which you need to come up with an AI-powered ICT product. The first stage is just a 2-page proposal of the idea which can be finished within one group meeting. Then near the end of semester, you need to make a 8-page proposal, which is just a detailed version of your stage one proposal, and prepare a 15-minute presentation. You can have up to 7 people in one group so the workload can be small if everyone shares participates.
The lab section has assignments, which can basically be finished in class so workload is low as well.

sections.content:
The course is comprehensive, covering the common topics in information technologies related to business. If you're interested in the TMT industry, you'll find this course helpful in building an overview of this industry.

Labs: Lab sessions also cover a lot of basic things, e.g., Excel formulas, database basics, and vibing a HTML... But honestly, what you can learn from the lab is far from practical skills in the workplace, as they are too basic.

Cons: Because it's just an introductory course, there isn't much depth in every topic. You cannot count on this course to give you some concrete know-how of them.
sections.teaching: Professor Dongwon is great. He can teach clearly and vividly, with a lot of examples discussed in class. He is also willing to discuss topics beyond the course with us.
sections.grading:
Because I'm familiar with those ICT concepts, an A+  is easy for me. Based on what I heard from my friends, Prof. Dongwon is quite generous in this course.

Class Participation 10% (4 in-class quizzes; you get full score as long as you submit them; the professor will remind you 1 lecture before)
Labs 15%
Midterm Exam 24%
Group Project 25% (Topic for this semester: design an AI digital product)
Final Exam 26%

Tips: For exams, focus on understanding concepts and the relationship among them, but do not memorize everything. Using AI to help generate a mind map is a good practice. (I attached a sample by Doubao - you may use other GenAI tools, but instructing them to be detailed is recommended.)

For the project, it's very important to make sure your ideas are aligned with the topic and requirements. And try to be innovative while feasible.
sections.workload: As long as you find responsible teammates, the workload is quite light. The only thing you need to spend extra time on is the project work -- one business model canva (2 pts), one pitch deck, one presentation (15pts for the deck and presentation), and one business plan (8pts). As responsible Generative AI use is allowed (as long as you don't fully rely on it and declare your use), I don't think it's a huge workload. And the project will be interesting for you if you're interested in product innovation.

Easy to score well if you attend her lectures. For participation she will always ask relatively easy questions and as long as you answer any one in her lecture, she will give you participation marks. For Labs, there are easy quizzes on Canvas every week with MCQs, I personally didn’t attend any lab sessions because attendance isn’t necessary. But just do the quizzes and you’ll be okay. For Group Projects, I highly recommend finding a group of people who are interested in the class, but it’s inevitable to have free-riders in your group. There’s a presentation pitch in which not everybody had to present in our group so if you don’t like presentations you can negotiate with your team members and contribute in some other way. Mid Term
Simple and Easy Mid Term Content. Generally, the class average should be quite high as the content is simple.

Project/Presentation
15 minutes Final presentation and Q&A at the end. Presentation format is very flexible, and can be creative.
- Research Question: Unique E-Commerce Model (very vague)
- Find a company that has a unique business model
- Effectiveness, and suitability of model --> Solutions?

Final Report
Report is a more detailed description of the presentation, include any pointers that you missed or would've wanted to address during the presentation.

Final Exam
The content in the final exam is mostly the second half of the course. However it is useful to have basic knowledge of the general concepts taught in the first half.

sections.content:
Content: C+

For the lecture part, there are basically 4 big topics:
1. Digital Economy
2. E-Commerce
3. Social Media
4. Big Data Analytics

The content for every professor is slightly different. For Professor Yang, he includes topics like Team, Strategy and Value Creation to help us preparing the group project. (But honestly the cotent is not that useful. I fell asleep or just watch YouTube videos...)

For the lab part, there are basically 4 topics:
1. Google manuels (Not tested)
2. Excels
3. VBA
4. SQL

You can refer the syllabus in the attached document.

Lecture part:

The content itself is very fundamental. You can understand almost all of them using common sense. Concepts like Metcalfe's Law, Moore's law, Web 2.0 are not taught deeply. Just introduce the basics and that's it.

The good thing is you don't need much brain power and time to revise them. The bad thing is you can't learn much and you feel like you learned something, but don't really know the significance and applications to the real world.

For Professor Yang, his lecture notes are pretty easy to comprehend and revise for the exam (some highlights and mind maps), although many slides are just pictures with no meaning.

Lab part:

The functions and codes are pretty fundamental for most of the parts. But even so, it is pretty challenging for those who have not learned anything related to IT before (like me...). Especially when all the concepts mix together at the end, it is very hard to understand them in a short period of time.

The lab manuels are ok for revision. But I recommend you to use AI to help you summarizing the content.
sections.teaching:
Teaching: B

He is mainland professor. His accent is pretty strong, but you can eventually get used to it after 2 weeks. His tone is a bit sleepy (but not as bad as other reviewers said).

It is the first time he teaching this course, so he may not be familiar with the teaching flow. However, I see he has tried his best to teach. For example, he would hold an exam review session beffore each exam. In the session, he would review the most improtant concepts, provide a mind map to connect different topics and indicate what topics are not tested. These are highly beneficial to our revision.

Also, he would try his best to simplify the content to make it less complicated. You can say this would make the content a bit less practical, but I think this is not that bad for the sake of the exam.

He also tried his best to make the class atmosphere more interactive by using Mentimeter to allow us to participate in the class. But it is not that useful to be honest.
sections.grading:
Grading: C+

Grading scheme:
Participation: 15%
Lab: 15%
Project: 20%
Midterm: 24%
Final exam: 26%

My results:
1. Participation: Full marks
2. Lab: Full marks
3. Project: 16/20
4. Midterm: 46/50 (Mean is around 28-30)
5. Final exam: ~ 80% (around UQ)

Total score: ~ 89%
Final grade: A-

The exam is pretty competitive especially in the final exam. Miss a few marks can already cause you to drop 1 subgrade. I may be able to get an A if I get a few more marks in the final exam. However, I am still very statisfied given I know nothing about the lab part before and one third of the students are from overseas.

Spoiler: Lecture exams are mostly MCQs, plus 1-2 short questions.  No need to write too much words.

I would not say it is a good grade course. As the content is pretty easy and only requires simple math, you must be very careful in order to avoid careless mistakes. No idea on the A-range precentage, but you can see getting 89% only resulting in A-. You can definitely know the A-range cut off is pretty high.

The group project is managable (15 minutes presentation + report), but you need to use the concepts taught as much as possible to let professor thinking you are not water-blowing. You can get 1 extra point if more people likes your presentation. (Doesn't matter in terms of your grade)

For the participation part, you need to participate by using Mentimeter to answer the question. Then, you need to provide proof and submit it on Canvas in order to gain participation points (I think you can skip 20% lectures, I forgot because the course is DELETED FROM CANVAS AFTER THE TERM...)

You also need to attend 2 talks in order to pass this course. The talks are ok.

Comments on Exams:
The exams test rote memorization rather than understanding or critical thinking. They aren't difficult, but require memorising almost everything from the 100-page exam review materials (the lecture slides can be skipped). Even trivial details are tested, such as the number of bitcoins generated per hour.

Comments on Grading:
On the bright side, the grading is comparatively generous. I highly recommend taking Lee Dong Won’s course, as in a poorly designed class like this, a good grade is really the best you can hope for.

Recommendation for future students:
First, make sure to find reliable groupmates (ideally, some who are confident presenters). For exam preparation, focus solely on memorising the material provided in the exam reviews; this approach maximises your score with minimal time investment. (Personally, I crammed everything 1–2 days before the exams.)

sections.teaching: Professor Lee's course is taught with a vibrant yet sometimes hard-to-follow Korean accent, requiring a few lectures to adjust. sections.grading:
Class Participation (15%):
Me: (15/15)
There are three aspects of your class participation.
First, be prepared and to participate in class activities(5%).
Second, students are also expected to contribute to other students learning (5%).
Third, students are also expected to attend the invited speakers’ sessions in the “Industry Week”. (5%).

Labs (15%):
Lab Quizzes: (5%)
Me: (5/5)
There is a lab quiz for each of the ten labs that students must complete and submit before mid-night on the same day they have the lab. Only the best nine lab quiz scores will count towards this 5% (the lowest one will be dropped).

Lab Final Exam: (10%)
Me: (8/10)
Lab final exam covers only Lab 2 to Lab 8, and is a separate paper taken consecutively with the lecture paper. This exam is around 30 minutes and has 20-30 questions. It is closed book, but a cheat sheet will be provided, and students cannot bring their own.

Group Project (20%):
Form a group of 7-8 students to work on a project at the beginning of the semester. The group is to develop a business idea for a new mobile application.
Three deliverables for the group project:
(1) the proposal (2%)
Me: 2/2
(2) the business plan(6%)
Me: 3.5/6
(3) the presentation (12%)
Me: 8/10

Midterm Exam (24%)
Me: 77/100
Average is 72.8 ; SD: 12.8
Final Exam (26%)
Me: 87.5/100
Average: 71; SD: 13
The exams will be based on the topics and related concepts taught during class. The midterm exam will test issues covered in the first half of the course. The final exam will cover the classes in the second half of the course.

Overall: A-

sections.grading:
Participation: 15/15, everybody should get full marks by joining the industry week and giving feedback on other groups presentation during the final three lessons. (I have tested it myself, just write “good” in the common board and you will get the participation score.)

mid-term (24%): 78/100, mean 72.8, sd 12.8, the paper was extremely poorly written, you have to recite every word in the PowerPoint, but only the 100 page long ppt named “mid term review” needs to be memorised, I didn’t know that and tried to memorise all the PowerPoint, wasted a lot of time but forgot a lot of things, resulting in an extremely poor score. (My friend got 92/100, didn’t sit any lesson and only memorised the mid term review)

Finals (26%): 83/100, mean 71, sd 13. This time the paper was even worse, but I managed to come back as I learnt the lesson from mid term. There were silly questions asking you about the number of bitcoins generated per hour. (3.125*6) However, an exam trick you could use is whether there’s “none of the above”, choose it. They just want to waste your time.

Lab (15%): 13.5/15 (with 5 marks being participation quizzes and 20 MCQs in the final exam, each weighs 0.5 mark), mean 10.5, sd 2.1. The lab is the only useful thing in this course, you get to learn about VBA and SQL.

Group project (20%): 16.5/20, first report 2/2, presentation 9/12, business plan 5.5/6, no stats so I actually don’t know if I performed well.

Total: 85.3/100, A, exceeded my expectation.
Although the exam questions are really bad, at least it can differentiate students, if you are hard-working and good at memorising thing you get a good grade, it’s better than Chen Yan Zhen’s class which the mean was 83 and a friend of mine got 88 and got a B, their mid term mean was 42/48 and a lot of people got 48, meaningless.

When you cannot learn anything in this course anyway, the only reason to take this course is to get good grades, so I will still suggest taking Lee Dong Won’s class as he said in the first class, “I don’t really care about giving more As to you, but you need to do well”

Class Participation (15%): There are two aspects of your class participation. First, students are expected to
participate in class activities (e.g., surveys, self-tests, reading assignments) and attend the invited speakers’
sessions in the “Industry Week” (5%). In-class participation (5%) - Providing answers to questions in the
Canvas discussion section is an effective approach. This not only enhances your own learning experience but
also fosters a more collaborative and interactive for everyone involved. The rest 5% is from the group peer
evaluation.
Note: Class participation does NOT include private discussions, e.g., after-class email correspondence.
Make-up policies: If you miss one of the attendance checks during the industry weeks, it is still possible to
partially make it up. Show the class one interesting video or case that relates to the most recent lecture topic and
provide brief comments to get 50% of the missing points back.
Labs (15%): The class environment of the lecture (e.g., big class size, no computer access) is not conducive for
teaching technical skills. Hence, there will be separate lab sessions of 50 minutes each to cover basic to advanced
skills. In almost every lab session, there is a task that you need to complete during the lab session. You MUST
attend the lab session to which you are assigned; lab instructors will ask unregistered students to leave. You
will not get credit for work done during a session for which you are not registered. Also, contents for
lectures and lab sessions are non-overlapping – generally, the lectures emphasize managerial and strategic
implications of information technology, whereas the lab sessions focus on specific technical knowledge.
Note: For attendance and all lab-related inquiries (class arrangements, exams and grades), please resort
to your lab instructions as the lab part is independent of the lectures.
Group Project (20%): This is a group-based course project that is intended to allow you to exercise your insights
and analytical abilities in a real-life business/industry. The group is to read about an emerging business
idea/industry with new technology (e.g., mobile application, blockchain, short video sharing platform) and
discuss its future trends, strategies, or impacts. The main deliverable is a set of slides detailing the technology,
the firm and industry summarized in the reading, potential questions identified from the reading and predictions
3
or suggestions. The groups need to apply what we discuss in class to their business ideas in identifying and
solving problems. A supplementary report provides explanations and evidence of the slides is expected.
We look for clarity, level of effort, and quality of content when assigning grades.
All members of a group would receive the same initial grade for the group project. The scores will be adjusted
according to peer reviews. Students who do badly in their peer evaluations in the group project would receive
lower grades for the second part of class participation.
Mid-term (20%) and Final (30%): These are major checkpoints to ensure that you understand the key concepts
that we introduce in this course. The mid-term examination will cover the Digital Economy and E-commerce
topics, whereas the final examination will cover materials of the other topics. Review sessions and catch-up
days will be scheduled to help you prepare for these examinations. In general, these examinations are non-
technical in nature. If you miss the midterm exam for an extreme emergency, you can have the final exam grade
count for both the missed midterm and the final. That one exam will thus constitute a greater portion of your
course grade. This extreme emergency must be approved by the instructor before the exam date, and counting
one exam twice is not a good idea!

Class Participation (15%): There are two aspects of your class participation. First, students are expected to participate in class activities (e.g., surveys, self-tests, reading assignments) and attend the invited speakers’ sessions in the “Industry Week” (5%). In-class participation (5%) - Providing answers to questions in the Canvas discussion section is an effective approach. This not only enhances your own learning experience but also fosters a more collaborative and interactive for everyone involved. The rest 5% is from the group peer evaluation.
Note: Class participation does NOT include private discussions, e.g., after-class email correspondence.

Make-up policies:  If you miss one of the attendance checks during the industry weeks, it is still possible to partially make it up. Show the class one interesting video or case that relates to the most recent lecture topic and provide brief comments to get 50% of the missing points back.

Labs (15%): The class environment of the lecture (e.g., big class size, no computer access) is not conducive for teaching technical skills. Hence, there will be separate lab sessions of 50 minutes each to cover basic to advanced skills. In almost every lab session, there is a task that you need to complete during the lab session. You MUST attend the lab session to which you are assigned; lab instructors will ask unregistered students to leave. You will not get credit for work done during a session for which you are not registered. Also, contents for lectures and lab sessions are non-overlapping – generally, the lectures emphasize managerial and strategic implications of information technology, whereas the lab sessions focus on specific technical knowledge.

Note: For attendance and all lab-related inquiries (class arrangements, exams and grades), please resort to your lab instructions as the lab part is independent of the lectures.

Group Project (20%): This is a group-based course project that is intended to allow you to exercise your insights and analytical abilities in a real-life business/industry. The group is to read about an emerging business idea/industry with new technology (e.g., mobile application, blockchain, short video sharing platform) and discuss its future trends, strategies, or impacts. The main deliverable is a set of slides detailing the technology, the firm and industry summarized in the reading, potential questions identified from the reading and predictions or suggestions. The groups need to apply what we discuss in class to their business ideas in identifying and solving problems. A supplementary report provides explanations and evidence of the slides is expected.

We look for clarity, level of effort, and quality of content when assigning grades.

All members of a group would receive the same initial grade for the group project. The scores will be adjusted according to peer reviews. Students who do badly in their peer evaluations in the group project would receive lower grades for the second part of class participation.

Mid-term (20%) and Final (30%): These are major checkpoints to ensure that you understand the key concepts that we introduce in this course. The mid-term examination will cover the Digital Economy and E-commerce topics, whereas the final examination will cover materials of the other topics. Review sessions and catch-up days will be scheduled to help you prepare for these examinations. In general, these examinations are non-technical in nature. If you miss the midterm exam for an extreme emergency, you can have the final exam grade count for both the missed midterm and the final. That one exam will thus constitute a greater portion of your course grade. This extreme emergency must be approved by the instructor before the exam date, and counting one exam twice is not a good idea!

Frankly, I think Professor CHEN truly knows a lot about information systems but her teaching is undoubtedly poor, here are some things to reference :)

Confusing announcements:

"Attention all ISOM2010ers!

There will be no courses on Feb-27 and Feb-29 (yep, we're as surprised as you are that it even exists this year).

Fear not, for make-up sessions will be conjured up in the not-so-distant future. Our next rendezvous? Mar-5 at our normal time. Until then, may your coffee be strong and your procrastination weak. "(????

Useless mock exams:

She sends three multiple choice questions before mid-term and final to Canvas as a mock exam to help us understand the exams better. However, her mock final is locked up right after you finish it without providing any results or answers. You can't check the mock question since it's locked up right after you submit it. The funniest part is that she later provided answers in an announcement, but the answers were totally wrong since she randomized the order of the three mock questions......

Terrible requirements are participation:

She required everyone who spoke in the class to sign their name after class, which led to some issues:
-Students would frequently raise their hands to answer questions, disrupting the flow of the lecture and preventing the instructor from covering the planned material.
-If students missed opportunities to answer questions during the class, they could simply ask random questions afterward in order to earn participation points. This resulted in many irrelevant or trivial questions being asked.
-Students could still sign the attendance sheet even if they had not actually spoken up in class, depending on their personal ethics.

sections.content:
Digital Economy:
1. Explain data, information, and information systems.
2. Know the meaning of Moore’s law, Metcalf’s law and their implications.
3. Understand the implications of globalization.
4. Discuss the use of information systems in organizations.
5. Describe the newer aspects of working in the digital world.
6. Define ethics and describe the major ethical problems posed by the digital world.

Ecommerce:
1. Describe the nature of e-business.
2. Define the e-business value chain and disintermediation.
3. Describe the basic e-business models.
4. Examine the major online marketing methods.
5. Discuss the major issues that are created by and affect e-business.

Social Media:
1. Describe the key component of social media.
2. Explain the 3 features of social media authoring.
3. Understand the meaning of Tagging.
4. Explain the differences between traditional and social media.

Technical Foundations:
1. Identify the major components of hardware and networking technology.
2. Identify the different types of software.
3. Describe the process in software development.
4. Discuss the trends in hardware and software, and the implications to businesses.

Big Data:
1. Explain how organizations use data and information.
2. Explain the basic concepts of data management (data creation, sharing, mining, reporting).
3. Define database management systems (DBMS) and describe their various functions.
4. Data storage within and across organizations.
5. Explain how the relational database model works.
6. Describe how databases are developed.
7. Explain how organizations can use data warehousing and data mining for decision making.
8. Describe advanced database models and when their use is appropriate.

Business Analytics and Decision Makings:
1. Discuss the problems associated with management decision-making.
2. Explain the specific information needs of managers in different functional areas of an organization,
including production, operations, marketing and sales, accounting, human resources and IT.
3. Explain the decision-making process.
4. Explain the increasing roles and responsibilities of accountants as user and owner of data and the
corporate information system.
5. Describe decision support systems.
6. Describe the opportunities and threats to corporate information system including capabilities in data
treatment and analysis, data integrity, system security and issues in access restriction, and business
contingency/continuity.
7. Discuss the roles and trend of IT in business analytics and decision making

Business, Accounting and Finance:
1. Formulate appropriate information systems strategies to support implementation of business and
functional strategies.
2. Use the system development life cycle to plan, design, implement, and evaluate an IT system.
3. Describe the application of information technology to accounting systems and the generation, reporting,
internal control and attestation of accounting information.
4. Recognize and understand the roles of accountants in all stages of the system development life cycle:
systems analysis; systems design; systems implementation; and systems operation and maintenance.
5. Demonstrate an understanding of the behavioral issues of implementing information systems in
organizations.
6. Describe how change management can contribute to successful implementation of information systems.

Technology-Enabled Business Trends:
1. Identify major tech-enabled trends in near future
2. Examine impact of tech-enabled trends on individuals, firms, and society
3. Discuss business opportunities of new technologies

sections.content:
It is a boring course, but if you work smart it is easy to get a good grade.

There are two parts to this course:
Lectures + Lab

For lectures, it depends if you wanna go or not. (and depends on if your prof takes attendance)
For the project, in my personal experience, I would suggest you to do as the professor said. As in, go and ask the prof for every little solution or problem you identify and see how they react to it. They are usually very welcome to questions and for Xu Hong, if you don't ask for her comments before the presentation she will ROAST you out irl and give you a very low grade. So make sure to be friendly to her so she will be more lenient on you during the Q&A of your presentation. FYI: your presentation doesn't take a lot in the grade, and she cares more about how you reply to her Q&A and the overall content of your project.

but STRONGLY SUGGEST YOU GO TO LAB by yourself in-person. they take attendance by quizzes so you can easily get answers from other people but if you learn the lab step-by-step with the tutor or you spend some time on your own to study it, you can easily get full marks on the lab paper in finals.
sections.teaching:
For Xu Hong, her lectures are very boring and the ppt isn't nice, but it is informative and will help you through midterm and finals even if you don't go to a single lesson!
(little hint: you can highlight the blank space below the questions on the ppt and copy&paste it out, I think a lot of ISOM profs do that and so you don't need to go to lectures for the answers)

Xu Hong doesn't really take attendance but make sure you attend the three talks during Industrial Week because that is the main contributor to her 'attendance' part of the grade.
sections.grading:
You get what you deserve.
I spent minimal amount of time in this course, only studied materials last minute (but I studied hard), spent most of the time asking professor questions to improve our project grade, went to every lab by myself and just recall everything you learn last minute before your finals.
That is all you need to get A+.
So work smart, and a little bit harder than other people.

1. Midterm
Just the content of lecture ppts, understand the highlighted words and key concepts and you'll be fine. Has both MCQ and Short Q.

2. Final
Once again, more lecture ppt content. This time more Short Q than MCQ but not too difficult. My advice would be to think of examples for different ideas and topics brought up in the course. A tiny bit of conditional probability is also included.

3. Project
Do research on a company and identify its strengths and weaknesses then talk about how your team would help elevate with the use of information systems. You will need to hand in a proposal, do a presentation and lastly submit a final report. Finding an appropriate business to write about is the tough part imo. Highly recommend booking office hours or consulting sessions to ask the prof if the current direction you're going is appropriate because through those sessions, you can understand what the prof wants to see in your projects. The professor will most likely question you after your preparations so be very prepared for that because Professor Xu's questions can be quite sharp which have left some groups incapable of giving a well thought out response. She will also make comments after the presentation which I'd recommend you mark down as you can make changes according to those comments for your final report.

4. Lab 5/15 +10/15
Do 10 all post-lab quizzes, all of them have unlimited tries and aren't that hard as long as you have gone to the lab or at least read the lab manual. This contributes to 5/15 marks for your lab component
The 10/15 marks for  your lab come from your "lab final exam" which is held on the same day as the final exam for your lecture content. Study up on the VBA and SQL stuff, those are crucial and will help you the most if you want to pursue a career in finance, IS, data analysis etc.

5. Participation
Industry talks and commenting on the presentations of your peers. She used the IPRS system once this whole semester, thank god I was there.

Overall comments :
From the amount of ? you see in my score, its kinda obvious that the grading is quite opaque. But regardless, I give grading an A because I felt like I did meh but still got A range which probably indicates a wide boundary for A range unlike some finance courses.

Overall, the course provides a broad and surface-level understanding of ISOM, covering content on digital technology, e-commerce, business analytics, platform business, big data, and cryptocurrency. On the other hand, the lab content is slightly more practical, covering basic VBA, Microsoft Access, and machine learning. The downside is that the TA does not explain the reasoning behind each step in detail. Overall, the course and lab content are not very useful, as they do not provide in-depth knowledge or skills. To put it in perspective, the lab material can be learned within a day, and the course content is simple and straightforward.
sections.teaching: It is hard to stay motivated to attend the classes, I missed most of the lectures since mid-term. The class is not very engaging, as the professor mostly reads from the PowerPoint slides, making it easy to lose focus. Additionally, the professor has a strong Korean accent, but fortunately, everything he says is on the slides, which makes it easier to understand. Some terms and theories are poorly explained, and the professor often paraphrases the concepts instead of adding new perspectives. However, both the professor and TAs are friendly and quick to respond to emails.

sections.content:
Course Description
In virtually every industry and every firm, information technology (IT) is driving change, creating opportunities and challenges. Leaders who don’t understand the fundamentals of information systems (IS) will be at a strategic disadvantage. IS have moved beyond the automation of back office functions, into the foreground of business strategy. IS play critical roles in competitive positioning and business process design.
This course provides broad coverage of technology concepts and social and economic trends underlying current and future developments in IT, and fundamental principles for the effective use of computer-based IS in businesses and other organizations. There will be a special emphasis on the digital economy, e-commerce, and business analytics. Other topics include: hardware/software, networking, the Internet, database, security, and social media. In additional to the fundamental conceptual and propositions in the IS area, a number of business applications and cases will be discussed. sections.content:
Digital Economy
1. Explain data, information, and information systems.  
2. Know the meaning of Moore’s law, Metcalf’s law and their implications.
3. Understand the implications of globalization.
4. Discuss the use of information systems in organizations.  
5. Describe the newer aspects of working in the digital world.  
6. Define ethics and describe the major ethical problems posed by the digital world.
Ecommerce
1. Describe the nature of e-business.  
2. Define the e-business value chain and disintermediation.  
3. Describe the basic e-business models.  
4. Examine the major online marketing methods.  
5. Discuss the major issues that are created by and affect e-business.

Social Media  
1. Describe the key component of social media.
2. Explain the 3 features of social media authoring.
3. Understand the meaning of Tagging.
4. Explain the differences between traditional and social media.

Technical Foundations
1. Identify the major components of hardware and networking technology.
2. Identify the different types of software.
3. Describe the process in software development.  
4. Discuss the trends in hardware and software, and the implications to businesses.
  ISOM 2010, Hong Xu
3
Big Data
1. Explain how organizations use data and information.  
2. Explain the basic concepts of data management (data creation, sharing, mining, reporting).
3. Define database management systems (DBMS) and describe their various functions.  
4. Data storage within and across organizations.  
5. Explain how the relational database model works.
6. Describe how databases are developed.  
7. Explain how organizations can use data warehousing and data mining for decision making.  
8. Describe advanced database models and when their use is appropriate.

Business Analytics and Decision Makings
1. Discuss the problems associated with management decision-making.  
2. Explain  the  specific  information  needs  of  managers  in  different  functional  areas  of  an  organization,  
including production, operations, marketing and sales, accounting, human resources and IT.
3. Explain the decision-making process.  
4. Explain  the  increasing  roles  and  responsibilities  of  accountants  as  user  and  owner  of  data  and  the  
corporate information system.
5. Describe decision support systems.  
6. Describe  the  opportunities  and  threats  to  corporate  information  system  including  capabilities  in  data  
treatment  and  analysis,  data  integrity,  system  security  and  issues  in  access  restriction,  and  business  
contingency/continuity.
7. Discuss the roles and trend of IT in business analytics and decision making

Business, Accounting and Finance
1. Formulate  appropriate  information  systems  strategies  to  support  implementation  of  business  and  
functional strategies.
2. Use the system development life cycle to plan, design, implement, and evaluate an IT system.
3. Describe the application of information technology to accounting systems and the generation, reporting,
internal control and attestation of accounting information.
4. Recognize and understand the roles of accountants in all stages of the system development life cycle:
systems analysis; systems design; systems implementation; and systems operation and maintenance.
5. Demonstrate  an  understanding  of  the  behavioral  issues  of  implementing  information  systems  in  
organizations.
6. Describe how change management can contribute to successful implementation of information systems.

Technology-Enabled Business Trends
1. Identify major tech-enabled trends in near future
2. Examine impact of tech-enabled trends on individuals, firms, and society
3. Discuss business opportunities of new technologies

Your grade depends on your performances in all the grading components. Just doing well in one or two components (e.g., mid-term and final lecture exams) does not mean you will get the top grade. Broadly speaking:

A-range (A+, A, A-): very good scores (e.g., close to top scores) in almost all the components.

sections.workload:
Too complicated, too many "little" things to do, easy to miss out 1 or 2 things

*Lecture Midterm Exam (40 mins) - T/F, MCQ, Short-answer questions - [Qualtrics]

*Lab Final Exam (25 mins) - Mix of multiple choice and fill in the blank questions - [Canvas]

*Lecture Final Exam (50 mins) - True/False, MCQ, Short-answer questions, SQL statements - [Qualtrics]

You will get TWO participation counts (also regarded as full credit) if you:
- Get TWO successful registration offers, attend TWO talks in person via Zoom; OR
- Get ONE successful registration offer, attend ONE talk in person via Zoom.
PLUS watching ONE video of ANOTHER talk and submit ONE reflection; OR
- Watching the videos of TWO talks and submit TWO reflections.

*Project presentation (10%) and report (10%)  -
the scores shown are the pre-moderated score. All students in the same group will get the same score. However, the actual project score that goes into your final course grade could be affected by the peer evaluation.

*Project presentation feedback:
- a total of 9 feedbacks + live attendance x 3 (excluded attendance during your turns to present)

1. Attendance is compulsory
- You attend your registered section "Live" for all presentations (even if you and/or your group is not presenting on that day).

2. Feedback submission
- Only those who are NOT presenting need to submit feedback on that day.
- Deadline: 11.59 PM HKT on the day of the presentation (D day).
- Quality of your feedback matters (part of the course grade; refer to course outline).

3. Feedback rating
- You must rate all the feedback for your group by 11.59 PM HKT the day after your presentation (D+1 day).
- Once every member in your group has rated all the feedback, all of you will be able to see my feedback and comment about your presentation.
- If your group has a non-responsive member who does not complete the ratings by D + 1 (causing the group to not see my feedback), inform me of the situation via email on D + 2 (i.e., 2 days after your presentation).

*Lab Quizzes -
10 quizzes, each carries 0.5 marks, a total of 5 marks counted towards the course grade

*Reading Assignments -
- Read an article and answer 2-3 questions [Qualtrics]

- 0 point if you did not submit anything

sections.content:
The course includes theorems about how business uses information, and examples such as crowd-funding, cryptocurrencies, google searching, etc. Quite a lot of small discussions in class (not counted to grades).

For lab session, Microsoft Excel, VBA, Access and basics of google machine learning (multi linear regression) are included.
sections.teaching:
1.5 hours lecture, 2 per week. Mostly reading powerpoint and watching related videos. Some class discussions on the topic. Before exam there will be a "revision guide", good enough if you follow the guide to prepare for the exam.

1 hour lab session per week (likely to overrun). Useful as introducing codes for VBA and Access.

Generally lecturers and TAs are nice and are willing (and capable) to answer students' questions.
sections.grading:
Attendence: Industry Talk (5%)
Lab quizzes (5%)
Midterm (20%)
Project (20% + 10% peer evaluation)
Final exam (30% lecture + 10% lab)

In the syllabus it is stated that 15% of grades are in class attendence, but actually 5% corresponds to industry talk (attend 2 talks that lasts about 2 hours each) and 10% in peer evaluation in group project, which means basically you can skip all classes if you like.

There are 10 lab quizzes in total, normally each having 5 MCs. Unlimited attempts are allowed so you can basically make it all correct.

Midterm and Final have very high mean as the questions are easy (around 80% - 85%)

Group project part is one big project to develop a product that uses information technology as the main part. A complete proposal report as well as financial budget and pitching powerpoint are needed. 5 people in a group and self-groupings are allowed.

As people having similar scores in midterm and final, if you make some careless mistakes in exams or fried up the group project, you will get a bad grade; but if you stand out a bit from others, you are close to A range.
sections.workload:
The heaviest part of workload is on the group project. It takes up 1 to 2 months for the whole process of idea generation, decide on product details, doing research and finally finalise a report. As self-grouping is allowed, better to get to know some friends before you join this class (it will be good if you are in a major and have some friends in the same major you know as they are likely to be preregistered in the same session).

Besides the main project, each week there is a lab quiz to be completed, which takes only about 5 to 30 minutes based on whether you really understand the content in lab session.

sections.content: He asked what we wanted to learn in the course and he really taught us about those topics that we were interested in.
sections.teaching: Neither boring but nor very interesting, he gave enough examples and explanations so it was not difficult to understand the topics.

mean = C+

sections.workload:

sections.content: You basically learn how an information system is being applied to business. For example, you get to know about Digital Economy, E-commerce, Online Platforms, Business Analytics, and Big Data Analytics. None of these topics really go in-depth though. You also get to learn some really easy programming skills in tutorials such as using Microsoft Access, Excel VBA ...... In the middle of the semester, you will also be attending industry talk and gain an insight of different business sectors from professionals working inside. Overall, it is quite an all-rounded course.
sections.teaching: The professor was okay. Her pronunciation sometimes is difficult to understand but overall I think it is acceptable. She also used a lot of examples in her teaching to illustrate the concepts.

The questions in the midterm and final were extremely easy and straightforward

sections.content:

It mainly introduces technology concepts and trends, including Digital Economy, E-commerce, Online Platforms, Business Analytics, Big Data Analytics and Financial Technology. The lab part would teach you some basic knowledge of Google Website, Excel, VBA, SQL and Big Data.
sections.teaching:
Because of the content, I always lose my concentration and play my mobile phone. But I would say Muller tries his best to explain concepts very detailedly and patiently with some examples. He is also willing to answer students' questions during and after class. So reg his lecture and you would never regret!

TA Samuel is also nice and patient. I think he is cute as he would use some interesting emojis when replying your emails.
sections.grading:
I don't know other professors, but Muller actually gives a good grade. Although I mess up my final, I still got an A.
Grading as follows:
Class Participation:
Industry week(5%): attend two talks and you can get full marks
Online Discussion(10%): 4 topics throughout the semester
Labs:
Lab Quiz(5%): 10 quizzes after attending labs, unlimited attempts, easy to get full marks
Lab Final10%): 20 minutes to finish 14 questions (MCQ and Fill-in-blank), due to the time limit, not easy
Group Project(20%): 12-minute-Presentation and 8-page-report. Think of a creative idea of an online platform/app, use concepts taught in class and you can get a satisfactory grade.
Midterm(20%): 50 minutes to finish 6 short essay questions
Final(30%): 30 minutes to finish 4 short essay questions, including SQL.
The exam is not cumulative.

I got full in participation, high in Midterm, above 0.5 sd in Lecture Final, 0.8sd in Lab Final, 18.4/20 in Group Project, turn out an A.
So the grade is SUPER GOOD.
sections.workload: The workload is moderate. Given the exam was both open-book, I didn't need to memorize concepts and saved lots of time. For group projects, my groupmates were SUPER good, so I did not spend too much time on the presentation and report. I would say the workload is OK.

sections.content:
Lecture:
[Midterm] Digital Economy, E-Commerce
[Lecture Final] Google and Online Platform, Social Media Management, Databases and Business Analytics, FinTech

Lab:
1 - Web Analytics (Google Sites & Google Analytics)
2 - Excel (Functions: AND, OR, IF, COUNTIF, SUMIF, VLOOKUP)
3-5 - Basic VBA (mostly learning structure of syntax)  
6-8 - Database using Microsoft Access
9-10: Big Data Analytics using Azure

Lecture exams are non-cumulative. Lab finals will test only knowledge from Labs 2-8. There will be an "Industry Week" in the middle of the semester to talk about IS stuff for 1h 30mins per talk.

Overall, lecture content is okay and lab content is pretty interesting.

For the lecture portion, this is purely a memorisation course. This semester was open-book because of online class. I asked the T.A. about why I did poorly in the midterm. Apparently, they grade based on markscheme so don't even bother with alternative explanations (e.g. from personal knowledge).

It's ironic how this course taught about "information overload" as one of the jargons, because it would be a representation of it.
sections.teaching:
Like with past reviews of this course and this professor, good luck trying to stay awake during lectures. I attended 100% of lectures so I can say that you'll be fine skipping like 80% of them. Accent is bearable, but professor reading from the slides is extremely boring. Kudos to the palpable effort though. Before the midterm and lecture final, there is a Q&A session so maybe attend that. For the midterm, sample MCQs were discussed in class so go to the last two sessions. For the lecture final, there were no practices, just the Q&A.

Professor's good when it comes to the ADP. Consult your ideas with her and try to make an impression, since scores for this component are undisclosed.

Contact T.A. Samuel if you want to ask about grades and some lab stuff. In-person checking is allowed but for online, he gives a breakdown of MCQ score and tips on the essay portion (based on experience asking for midterm).

Really enjoyed T.A. Olivia Chan who was assigned to my Lab. She is kind and energetic during labs, while being responsive to e-mails in terms of both time and comprehensiveness (which really helps for the lab finals).

Course has high means. Like in previous years, scores on the ADP are undisclosed. It's probably just based on the effort you put because the grading criteria is truly questionable (imagine a 3-page report with TNR 12 and double-spacing; idk how anyone can be comprehensive enough). I believe that final grade is consistent to previous years' grading, so fair enough.
sections.workload:
Light workload overall. Weekly labs aren't too difficult. Industry Week just requires either attendance or a 250-word reflection paper for full marks.

ADP consists of 5-6 people, with the liberty to choose groupmates. It's fine as long as you're not with free-riders.

The workload is just reserved to familiarising yourself with the lab final content. In a physical semester, this would be memorising every concept for both midterm and lecture final. However, in an online semester, just remember where each concept is in your notes and then copy explanations word-for-word.

Also don't take coding SQL for-granted. I have reason to believe that exams from previous years are just repeated, so listen to previous years' reviews. Learning this hits two birds with one stone for the Database topic in both lecture and lab finals.

sections.teaching:

Anyway, this turns out to be a great decision!

As a person who has come across 2 professors' teaching, here is an honest comparison: Muller>>>Chen.

Even though it is the first year (I believe) that Muller taught ISOM2010, his teaching is really great and accent is much more understandable than Chen (makes a huge diff here cos you can barely learn anything from chen's class with her accent). sections.content:
Digital Economy
1. Explain data, information, and information systems.
2. Know the meaning of Moore’s law, Metcalf’s law and their implications.
3. Understand the implications of globalization.
4. Discuss the use of information systems in organizations.
5. Describe the newer aspects of working in the digital world.
6. Define ethics and describe the major ethical problems posed by the digital world.
Ecommerce
1. Describe the nature of e-business.
2. Define the e-business value chain and disintermediation.
3. Describe the basic e-business models.
4. Examine the major online marketing methods.
5. Discuss the major issues that are created by and affect e-business.
Social Media
1. Describe the key component of social media.
2. Explain the 3 features of social media authoring.
3. Understand the meaning of Tagging.
4. Explain the differences between traditional and social media.
Technical Foundations
1. Identify the major components of hardware and networking technology.
2. Identify the different types of software.
3. Describe the process in software development.
4. Discuss the trends in hardware and software, and the implications to businesses.
ISOM 2010, Hong Xu
3
Big Data
1. Explain how organizations use data and information.
2. Explain the basic concepts of data management (data creation, sharing, mining, reporting).
3. Define database management systems (DBMS) and describe their various functions.
4. Data storage within and across organizations.
5. Explain how the relational database model works.
6. Describe how databases are developed.
7. Explain how organizations can use data warehousing and data mining for decision making.
8. Describe advanced database models and when their use is appropriate.
Business Analytics and Decision Makings
1. Discuss the problems associated with management decision-making.
2. Explain the specific information needs of managers in different functional areas of an organization, including production, operations, marketing and sales, accounting, human resources and IT.
3. Explain the decision-making process.
4. Explain the increasing roles and responsibilities of accountants as user and owner of data and the corporate information system.
5. Describe decision support systems.
6. Describe the opportunities and threats to corporate information system including capabilities in data treatment and analysis, data integrity, system security and issues in access restriction, and business contingency/continuity.
7. Discuss the roles and trend of IT in business analytics and decision making
Business, Accounting and Finance
1. Formulate appropriate information systems strategies to support implementation of business and functional strategies.
2. Use the system development life cycle to plan, design, implement, and evaluate an IT system.
3. Describe the application of information technology to accounting systems and the generation, reporting, internal control and attestation of accounting information.
4. Recognize and understand the roles of accountants in all stages of the system development life cycle: systems analysis; systems design; systems implementation; and systems operation and maintenance.
5. Demonstrate an understanding of the behavioral issues of implementing information systems in organizations.
6. Describe how change management can contribute to successful implementation of information systems.
Technology-Enabled Business Trends
1. Identify major tech-enabled trends in near future
2. Examine impact of tech-enabled trends on individuals, firms, and society
3. Discuss business opportunities of new technologies

The previous part of the course is about the use of information system in different businesses, she provided a lot of examples of company using information system to create change in the market.

sections.grading:
There is 1 midterm and group project, as well as final exam.

Both the midterm and final exam are divided into 2 parts: MC and Short Questions. Short questions are easy, just a dictation of lecture notes. However, the MCs are critical to your grade because they takes 6 marks per question in midterm and 3 marks per question in final exam.

In the final exam, there is also a lab section that examine all the knowledge taught in the lab session.

The Application Development Project is to propose a business idea which leverage the advantage of mobile application. You have to apply some knowledge and analyzing tools in lectures. Generally, you get high marks if you spend enough time on it, grades are not deviated in this part.

Therefore, you can score high marks if you spent enough time to understand and remember the terms and jargon in the lecture notes.

sections.teaching:
Professor Baek Jiye is a new professor in HKUST. I don't think she had much teaching experience, so her first few lessons were either too long or too short due to bad planning and time management. However, her teaching got much better towards the end of the semester. She delivers any main point in a good manner, and her powerpoint slides were organized and easy to follow.

Her voice is quite soft. I took her 9am lecture, and believe me, as a student without a hall, you will definitely fall asleep in her lesson. On the other hand, she listens to students' opinions and tries to improve her teaching in the process. When some students pointed out that her voice was too soft, she brought a louder mic in the following lesson in the hopes that we will be satisfied. Although I would not say she is the best professor as she still has a lot of room for improvement, I appreciate her attitude towards students and teaching.
sections.grading:
She's a new professor, as I mentioned, so her grading was the most unpredictable out of the 3 professors who taught in 2018/19 spring (Koh Tat Koon and Chen Yanzhen). In the beginning, I would expect that her grading will follow the 20%-40%-40% guideline strictly.

After I received my grade, I would only say the grading is fair. Her grading is not exceptionally bad, at least from my perspective. Here are my stats in examinations:
Midterm: above mean ~0.5sd
Final: below mean ~0.5sd
Lab: maximum (above mean ~1sd)
Attendance: all full except I missed one reflection on industry week
Project: around mean (slightly below)
Participation: should be full, stat not provided

Final Grade: B

I think it is quite fair. However, I heard from someone from the 10:30 session, where he/she got a mean score on essentially everything and got a C-. I also heard others saying that the mean is on C range. Unpredictable. I guess I was lucky?
sections.workload:
I would say a normal workload for a 3 credit course. There are no assignments and quizzes. There's only 1 midterm and then a final for examinations. And then there's a project, which consists of a proposal (2%), presentation (10%) and a business plan (8%). Towards the end of the semester, the workload noticibaly increased as you would need to complete the presentation and business plan within like 2 weeks.

Also, you would need to attend a 1-hour long lab session every week on top of your normal lecture. The lab session, unlike the lecture, is compulsory and attendance is required. You would need to spend more lesson time compared with a normal business core course, which does not have any labs/tutorials.

Study Guides as following:
For EXAMS:
- the course does not really cover a lot of contents, so exams would typically not be lengthy. So be extra Cautious to every detail in exam (make sure you mastered the limited lecture materials beforehand), since each wrong answer would lead to great deduction in marks.

For PROJECT:
- Typically every group would perform averagely well, so as the final score. But do remember to apply ISOM concepts in your project report and presentation (as well have a good relationship and bonding with your teammates! Peer evaluation is included in the grade review)

For LAB:
- For better and more efficient understanding of the lab session, do the pre-reading of class material before each class. Actually the content was not that difficult, everyone ended up with decent marks in the LAB final exam.

I ended up with an A.

sections.content:
In virtually every industry and every firm, information technology (IT) is driving change, creating opportunities and challenges. Leaders who don’t understand the fundamentals of information systems (IS) will be at a strategic disadvantage. IS have moved beyond the automation of back office functions, into the foreground of business strategy. IS play critical roles in competitive positioning and business process design.
This course provides broad coverage of technology concepts and trends underlying current and future developments in IT, and fundamental principles for the effective use of computer-based IS in businesses and other organizations. There will be a special emphasis on the digital economy, e- commerce, and business analytics. Other topics include: hardware/software, networking, the Internet, database, security, and enterprise applications. In additional to the fundamental conceptual and propositions in the IS area, a number of business applications, cases, and the newest trend in today’s technology domain will be discussed.

E-Commerce

Business Analytics

Emerging Technology

sections.teaching:
Try to sit in front of the class because it will be easy to fall asleep in her class for two reasons: 1. her tone can be quite boring 2. it is a big LT so sitting further back will get you distracted.

however, when it comes to class presentations Q&A time, she is extremely sharp which makes you think a lot about your business idea (final class project was to develop a business idea using an emerging technology). I love her questions as they are all very challenging. P.s. if you make pretty slides, she will like it very much!
sections.grading:
Wasn't too sure on the grading curve as I didn't really track it but overall A+. I think this was due to two reasons:

1. I studied for the midterm and final by compiling all her lecture notes together into one document (20/30 pages long). Just copy and paste them because her slides are all in PPT with different sizes so making them into one WORD document with one font size was much better for revision. The midterm & final content didn't deviate much from classroom notes.

2. I studied really hard for the coding parts of the LAB sessions. If you want to ensure you get an overall A grade, DO NOT SKIP  YOUR REVISION OVER THE LAB SESSIONS. REPEAT- MAKE SURE YOU UNDERSTAND THE STUDY GUIDE. This is the make-it-or-break-it for finals, not the classroom notes.

3. ATTEND the midterm and final review sessions. It's actually all that was necessary for me, at least for students who like to skip class.
sections.workload: No homework, so its quite light. The projects can be a bit tough if you change it midway so try to think strategically when selecting your idea for the project since you will be doing it the whole term. Besides, there will be 1-2 impromptu iLearn quiz that she will have but it is super easy.

sections.content:
As somebody else here has said, basically an introduction to consultancy or strategic management instead of information system. Maybe it's useful for case coms, but I believe this course isn't designed to prepare us for case coms... If a huge chunk of the whole course is just packed with the so-called "managerial insights" without the most basic technical detail, it's misleading in the sense that it's telling us as if IS major does not involve much technical stuff.

 Digital Economy
 E-Commerce
 Online Platforms
 Social Media
 Software
 Hardware
 Databases and Business Analytics
 Big data
 Crowdsourcing

 IT Fundamentals
 IT Trends

The lab section is slightly more relevant. We're introduced with business analytics using Excel VBA and big data analytics using Microsoft Azure. But you need a little bit of statistics background (e.g. simple linear regression, the concept of R-square, etc) to better understand what the heck is going on.

 Google Web Analytics
 Microsoft Access Database Management
 Business Analytics with Microsoft Excel
 Advanced Business Analytics with Excel VBA
 Big Data Analytics with Microsoft Azure

Overall the course could have been better structured to reflect and give us a preview of how the IS major is like.
sections.teaching:
Probably Tat Koon is limited by the crappy design of the course content, but I'm afraid to say that his lectures really add no values to enhancing our understanding of the course materials. He has a tendency to over-explain simple stuff and initiates discussion on issues that are already trivial to most of us. That's why I decided to skip almost all lectures after the midterm.

The most disappointing part is how he handled the course console issue. He could have easily known that the server couldn't handle such a large course when he picked a plan in which the max_connection parameter is merely 30. (WTF??) Throughout the whole process he reacted in a way hoping the situation would "automatically" get better by extending deadlines, but every one of us knew that the minor stuff couldn't solve the problem at all. It wasn't until the third round of presentation when he came up with a more reasonable solution of utilizing the Google Forms to replace the course console. Thanks to his "timely" response a lot of us stayed in front of our laptops the whole night refreshing the course console website in frustration (which worsened the situation).

Btw the hidden messages in his ppt are just words in white that can be easily revealed by a PDF editor like Adobe Acrobat.

On the other hand, the lab TA has an annoying Hong Kong Chinglish accent and a mosquito-like sharp voice that drives you nuts. But other than her English proficiency everything else is fine.
sections.grading:

 15% Labs
 20% Group project

 25% Final exam

Absurd non-sense. 15% out of the 20% class participation is based on how the other project groups rated your feedback of their own presentations. (Read: NEVER give low marks to them even if their work is sh!t, or they revenge by giving you a low rating in return) The other 5% is basically the online assignments that are posted on Canvas "secretly", i.e. you don't even know the existence of the assignments if you don't check the Canvas regularly. The assignments are basically a piece of cake for us, but since nobody ever mentions that the assignments are released, if you miss them, you lose the marks. You're graded based on whether you check the Canvas or not.

Tat Koon claimed that he aimed to increase the weighting of the group project and decrease the weighting of exams, but he beat his own mouth by giving us more or less similar scores in the group project. As it turned out exams were still the dominant factor that differentiated A's, B's and C's. The group project? In IS terms, non-negotiable but also a non-differentiator of your grade. Just finish the project. DON'T put too much effort into it.

We were also somehow misled into thinking that the lab final exam was a part the 25% of the final exam, but it turned out that it was 10% out of the 15% of the lab part. Thus actual weighting of all exams combined is 55%, more important than it seems.

Midterm
Mean = 28.2/34. SD = 3. I got 1.13 SD above mean.

Final
Mean = 38/49. SD = 6.8. I got around 1.25 SD above mean.

Lab final
Mean = 38.7/50. SD = 6.9. I got around 1.35 SD above mean.

Project presentation
Our group was one of the groups that scored the minimum, but it was still a 9/10. The highest was 9.8. With such small standard deviation, it doesn't really matter whether your group did well or not in the project.

I believe all of us were taken by surprise with such a technically oriented final exam. mySQL was heavily tested and the proportion of long questions asking on those managerial insights were greatly reduced.

Benefiting from this exam-oriented grading scheme, I got an A at the end.

Btw there is no correlation between active participation in class and the final grade. I got an A even though I am an introvert that never spoke up in class, and I skipped a lot of lessons as well.

sections.content: The content is not interesting at all, I cannot learn anything from the lectures. For example, he talked about big data and how to use them, but he did not actually talk about how we can have access to such data or the methods or software that we can use to analyze the data. There are a lot of concepts which we can seldom apply to real life. His group projects are also extremely meaningless and I learnt nothing from it. He tried to have us to include some IS concepts in the development of the app, but those concepts will no longer be included in the final exam so it actually helps us nothing towards our learning.
sections.teaching: His powerpoint is so useless that we can hardly access the information we need for exam. Sometimes he will hide some key concepts or information and we must attend his lectures in order to get the missing part of the powerpoint. Yet, his lectures are actually extremely boring and not fun at all. He asks quite a number of questions but actually only international students will answer the questions. He does not even try to help local students to engage or to be involved more in the lectures deliberately. Moreover, his comment giving to group presentations, which is supposed to be the most useful for the groups for their final reports, are even shorter than those written by other students. I expected so much from his comments but turned out it did not help me even for any little bit.
sections.grading: I worked so hard for the mid-term exam but I still got below-mean, I seriously doubt that he only gives good grades to international students, and local students are the ones to suffer. His grading also depends a lot on the class participation. Although he says that class participation will not matter a lot on the grades, I am quite sure that he has weighting on the students' score (he claimed that he has upgraded all students' grades by multiplying each student's score by a certain constant) based on their participation. It is very unfair for people who are not that active but still worked hard on the exams.
sections.workload: There is not much to do so there is no place for us to exercise what we have learnt. We may apply the wrong concepts on the exams but we have no way to know as there is no homework to practise our learnings. He is too lazy to put up any homework but yet have the time and effort to make his own website, which does not work most of the time. Even when it works, it is loading at an extremely low speed. I expect him to put some homework on his website. Moreover, he put up some reading assignments but do not have any announcement to remind us to do the work. Contents are very easy and basic. It grants students chances to have a look at what Information System is in fact. To me personally, it is an eye-opening experience as I really understand more about Information System and I am attracted by the course that I am going to go for this major.
sections.teaching: Dr. P stresses on class atmosphere and interaction of students and teachers. He played many interesting IS-related videos and allowed students to discuss among some open-ended topics. Discussion occupies quite a large portion of the lecture period. His teaching is systematic, interesting and inspiring.
sections.grading: Since course materials are quite easy, it is relatively difficult to get good grades even if we did a great job in final and projects. One mark matters a lot in ISOM 2010. You have to engage more in lesson so that he can recognise you and remember your name and score higher for participation.
sections.workload: Small workload, only a short project to hand in and present at the end of the course plus two midterms and a final. Only very few things have to be revised and memorised. His midterms and final are like dictation.

sections.content: The content itself is pretty straightforward - digital economy, e-commerce, big data, business analytics. There's no textbook, and all the required information is found on the lecture slides, which are pretty detailed and easy to follow.
sections.teaching: Professor Zhang is a really interactive and interesting teacher, and you learn a lot from him - both about the content and about wider issues in class. He's very helpful and it's very easy to approach him with any questions you have with the course content, group project and anything else. I would highly recommending enrolling in his section because his lessons are very interesting.
sections.grading:
Grading is pretty decent. There's a group project, attendance (randomly counted), midterm and final. Be warned though, the mean for the midterm and final is really high because the exams themselves are quite simple (for example, the mean for the midterm was 85/100 with SD 6.5 or so). So, taking that into respect, it's not THAT easy to get A range. That said, Professor Zhang tries to give as many students grades in the A range, so your hard work should be reflected in your grade.

In addition, there are also weekly tutorials and the content covered in the later lab sessions is assessed in a lab paper that is given during the final exam session. Lab session attendance and lab paper grades counts for 15% of the total grade.
sections.workload: Workload is extremely light. As you are allowed to form your own group for the project, it is pretty flexible and if you are teamed up with hard workers, the project isn't too difficult to complete (but it is important that your idea is unique/innovative if you are doing the app). Other than that, attending all the lectures should be sufficient and in case you're not able to attend any of them, all of the lectures are videotaped and posted on Canvas incase you want to watch them again for review.

sections.content:
Digital Economy
1. Explain data, information, and information systems.
2. Know the meaning of Moore’s law, Metcalf’s law and their implications.
3. Understand the implications of globalization.
4. Discuss the use of information systems in organizations.
5. Describe the newer aspects of working in the digital world.
6. Define ethics and describe the major ethical problems posed by the digital world.
Ecommerce
1. Describe the nature of e-business.
2. Define the e-business value chain and disintermediation.
3. Describe the basic e-business models.
4. Examine the major online marketing methods.
5. Discuss the major issues that are created by and affect e-business.
Social Media
1. Describe the key component of social media.
2. Explain the 3 features of social media authoring.
3. Understand the meaning of Tagging.
4. Explain the differences between traditional and social media.
Technical Foundations
1. Identify the major components of hardware and networking technology.
2. Identify the different types of software.
3. Describe the process in software development.
4. Discuss the trends in hardware and software, and the implications to businesses.
Big Data
3
1. Explain how organizations use data and information.
2. Explain the basic concepts of data management (data creation, sharing, mining, reporting).
3. Define database management systems (DBMS) and describe their various functions.
4. Data storage within and across organizations.
5. Explain how the relational database model works.
6. Describe how databases are developed.
7. Explain how organizations can use data warehousing and data mining for decision making.
8. Describe advanced database models and when their use is appropriate.
Business Analytics and Decision Makings
1. Discuss the problems associated with management decision-making.
2. Explain the specific information needs of managers in different functional areas of an organization, including production, operations, marketing and sales, accounting, human resources and IT.
3. Explain the decision-making process.
4. Explain the increasing roles and responsibilities of business managers as user and owner of data and the corporate information system.
5. Describe decision support systems.
6. Describe the opportunities and threats to corporate information system including capabilities in data treatment and analysis, data integrity, system security and issues in access restriction, and business contingency/continuity.
7. Discuss the roles and trend of IT in business analytics and decision making
Business, Accounting and Finance
1. Formulate appropriate information systems strategies to support implementation of business and functional strategies.
2. Use the system development life cycle to plan, design, implement, and evaluate an IT system.
3. Describe the application of information technology to various business fields including marketing, accounting, finance, strategic management and operations management.
4. Demonstrate an understanding of the behavioral issues of implementing information systems in organizations.
5. Describe how change management can contribute to successful implementation of information systems.
Technology-Enabled Business Trends
1. Identify major tech-enabled trends in near future
2. Examine impact of tech-enabled trends on individuals, firms, and society
3. Discuss business opportunities of new technologies

sections.content: The syllabus is very well-designed in the sense that the topics are grouped into three to four themes, which makes it super easy to understand the logic flow within each of them. Regarding the materials, there is no required textbook but handouts, so no need to worry about buying expensive books for a good grade. Everyone is supposed to be on the same page in the beginning.
sections.teaching: The professor is very passionate in teaching students. He always moves in front of the whiteboard to allow students in different corners of the classroom to speak up, making the lectures as interactive as possible.

sections.workload: I think in general this course's workload is rather light. Students need not prepare too much (except your brain) for every lecture. No (pop-up/scheduled) quizzes. However, when the time comes (i.e. as the deadline for group presentation is approaching), students usually feel quite stressed out. Frequent meetings and rehearsals are needed. One suggestion is to start brainstorming and consolidating the group ideas as early as possible.

sections.content:
You will learn about what makes services such as social media websites and platforms (like this one) work - along with a lot of theories, real-life examples, and most importantly - future trends. (because otherwise you really could have read the book called Information Rules. It's a good book entailing some basic principles behind technological development and etc. You'll hear him recommending it as well)

There are also 10 lab sessions. Highly recommended not just for attendance score, but also some are quite useful, esp the pivot table.
sections.teaching:
Understandably this course has to be taught by passionate and friendly instructors, because it has to be used to lure people into the major (oops).  

TK is very insistent on encouraging participation in class, so please raise your hand to answer/ ask questions.  There are also some discussions in class based on what you've just learnt and some info that he was showing (usually real-life cases).  Of course, you do not want to use these opportunities to bs because you can train your critical thinking <-- something he values a lot (just saying)

Timture teaches the lab sessions.  He's VERY friendly and very willing to answer your questions.  If you follow his instructions you can breeze through it with no problem.  Also, if you don't like hearing Cantonese accent in English, either deal with it or register in another session.
sections.grading:
I consistently get slightly below mean scores in my midterm and final exam - I know I'm very bad at taking exams.  At least that did not stop me from getting an A- with the project score being quite good and participation being (top 15% of class - according to TK's email).

Now does that make you want to work hard for good grades and recognition? I hear these things boost self-esteem a lot :D
sections.workload:
Typically the workload is light: it has a midterm, final exam, one reading material (but he gave 2 questionnaires/ "assignments" for that), and a project (presentation + report).  The reading material was around 4 pages long, but I heard that some people wrote that they'd like to have more reading materials so I'm not sure if the load would become heavier next time it comes...

The workload could become heavy if your project groupmates 1. freeride, 2. don't agree with each other, or 3. somehow cannot understand what's happening with the idea that you (or another person) proposed - exactly what happened to my group...
